title: Riverton Court Maintenance Atlas
summary: A realistic 64-unit apartment maintenance plan organized into nested views for systems, safety, inspections, emergencies, capital planning, vendors, and records.
audience: Apartment property managers, maintenance supervisors, asset managers, and operations teams who need a practical building map instead of a flat checklist.

data.title: Riverton Court
data.detail: 64 apartments, four floors, one elevator, central hot water, split HVAC, flat roof, parking, laundry, trash room.

data.title: Year-Round Care
data.detail: Treat the building as a living system: inspect, document, correct, and learn before issues become emergencies.

data.title: Resident Safety
data.detail: Life-safety, habitability, egress, heat, water, and communication outrank cosmetic work.

data.title: Proof and Records
data.detail: Every inspection, vendor visit, photo, deficiency, and correction needs a durable place in the record.

data.text: Use this as a realistic apartment maintenance map: start broad, open a domain, then drill into one system, procedure, inspection, or record pack.

data.title: Property Facts
data.detail: Built 1986. Four stories. 64 units. Elevator. Central domestic hot water. No on-site manager overnight.

data.title: Building Stack
data.detail: Ground: lobby, laundry, trash. Floors 2-4: apartments. Roof: drains, exhaust, make-up air, antenna.

data.title: Resident Profile
data.detail: Families, older residents, shift workers, pets, delivery traffic, and accessibility needs shape maintenance timing.

data.text: This view keeps orientation data close to the work. Every emergency flow and vendor visit depends on fast access to addresses, shutoffs, keys, and site constraints.

data.title: Front Entrance
data.detail: Main callbox, package shelf, lobby camera, fire panel, resident notices, and primary key box.

data.title: Service Entry
data.detail: Trash room door, loading zone, janitor closet, vendor sign-in, and after-hours access route.

data.title: Parking and Drainage
data.detail: Catch basins, snow pile zones, pothole tracking, lighting coverage, and tow/fire-lane markings.

items.text: Clear fire lane and hydrant access
Check exterior lights and trip hazards
Inspect trash enclosure and bulk items
Look for ponding water or blocked drains

data.text: A site map is not decoration here. It is the operational memory for access, response time, resident impact, and recurring exterior issues.

data.title: Water Main
data.detail: Mechanical room west wall. Tag valve, keep handle clear, and record every emergency shutoff.

data.title: Gas and Electric
data.detail: Meter room and main electrical panels require clear working space and controlled vendor access.

data.title: Fire System Valves
data.detail: Riser room valves, gauges, tamper switches, and drain paths need protection from storage creep.

items.text: Staff know who can operate each shutoff

data.text: Do not improvise during a leak, outage, or alarm. This child view keeps locations, authority, and documentation duties together.

data.title: Cadence Rule
data.detail: Recurring maintenance owns the calendar. Emergency work interrupts it, but should not erase it.

data.text: The calendar is organized by risk and frequency, not by department. That makes it easier to spot neglected systems before they become resident complaints.

items.text: Walk lobby, stairs, laundry, trash, and parking
Clear egress paths and blocked doors
Log urgent leaks, heat, lock, and safety calls
Check exterior lighting after dark weekly

data.title: Work Triage
data.detail: Separate emergencies, habitability, scheduled repairs, cosmetic work, and capital issues at intake.

data.title: Housekeeping Signals
data.detail: Trash, odors, pests, clutter, and water marks often reveal system problems before residents report them.

data.text: Daily walks protect the building from slow drift: storage in stairwells, failed lights, blocked drains, and small leaks.

items.text: Smoke and CO alarm sample checks

data.title: Backlog Review
data.detail: Look for repeated unit lines, unresolved vendor tickets, missing photos, and stalled resident communication.

data.text: Monthly and quarterly reviews connect field observations with records. A checklist without follow-up is only a snapshot.

items.text: Fall: heat startup, windows, leaf drains
Winter: freeze protection, ice control, backup heat plan
Storm season: resident notices and supplies

data.title: Proof Pack
data.detail: Photos, dates, vendor reports, and correction notes make seasonal work visible months later.

data.text: Seasonal maintenance is where operational planning and capital planning meet: the same roof leak can be a repair today and a replacement signal tomorrow.

data.title: Health and Safety First
data.detail: Use HUD NSPIRE as a practical lens: health, safety, functional defects, and year-round maintenance.

data.title: Local Code Check
data.detail: Confirm adopted property maintenance, fire, elevator, and rental inspection rules with the local authority.

data.title: Evidence Binder
data.detail: Keep inspection reports, deficiency corrections, photos, resident notices, vendor reports, and dates together.

items.text: Verify records and certificates are current
Assign one owner for deficiency closure

data.text: The goal is not to prepare at the last minute. The goal is to make inspection readiness the normal state of the building.
Life-safety work needs fast visibility across roles. This view separates fire systems, escape paths, and elevator obligations without losing the building-level picture.

data.title: Fire Alarm
data.detail: Panel status, monitoring account, annual inspection, trouble signals, pull stations, horns/strobes, and deficiency reports.

data.title: Sprinklers and Standpipe
data.detail: Riser room access, valves, gauges, drains, five-year items, impairment steps, and licensed inspections.

data.title: Extinguishers
data.detail: Monthly visual check, annual service tags, correct mounting, clear access, and replacement tracking.

data.title: Smoke and CO Alarms
data.detail: Unit and common-area device checks, battery policy, resident reporting, and replacement dates.

data.text: Reference lens: NFPA 25 for water-based fire protection ITM, NFPA 72 for alarm ITM, plus local fire marshal requirements.

data.title: Stairwells
data.detail: No storage, no propped doors, working closers, handrails intact, lighting adequate, tread hazards corrected.

data.title: Corridors
data.detail: Clear width, no trip hazards, functioning lights, visible unit numbers, and resident notice boards managed.

data.title: Exterior Exits
data.detail: Snow/ice control, panic hardware, door sweep condition, lighting, and landing drainage.

items.text: Walk each stair top to bottom

data.text: Egress is a habit, not a file. Blocked paths and failed lighting are visible defects that can become severe quickly.

data.title: Service Contract
data.detail: Monthly service, callback terms, parts exclusions, emergency phone, and response time expectations.

data.title: Certificates
data.detail: Annual inspection records, deficiency corrections, jurisdiction filings, and posted permit/certificate status.

data.title: Outage Plan
data.detail: Resident notices, mobility support, vendor escalation, manager coverage, and after-hours communication.

items.text: Ride car and listen for issues

data.text: Elevator rules vary by jurisdiction. This view keeps owner duties, contractor work, inspections, and resident impact in one place.

data.title: Systems Rule
data.detail: A failed building system usually creates work in multiple views: resident impact, vendor call, record, and capital signal.

data.title: Domestic Hot Water
data.detail: Boilers/tanks, circulation pumps, mixing valves, sample points, temperature log, and scald controls.

data.title: Leak Response
data.detail: Stop water, protect electrical, notify affected residents, dry materials, photograph, and track root cause.

data.title: Sewer and Drains
data.detail: Main cleanouts, stack history, floor drains, roof drains, catch basins, and recurring backup locations.

data.title: Water Quality Risk
data.detail: Complex water systems need temperature control, flushing after low use, and a responsible water-management team.

data.text: Reference lens: EPA and CDC-oriented Legionella guidance recommends water management programs for multifamily and complex building water systems.

data.title: Equipment Inventory
data.detail: Unit heat pumps, make-up air, exhaust fans, thermostats, filters, age, model, warranty, and access notes.

data.title: Filters and Belts
data.detail: Replacement cadence, resident access limits, rooftop safety, contractor scope, and evidence photos.

data.title: Exhaust and Ventilation
data.detail: Bath fans, kitchen exhaust, corridor pressurization, odors, humidity, and airflow complaints.

data.text: Reference lens: ASHRAE multifamily guidance focuses on HVAC operation, maintenance, ventilation, and airflow.

data.title: Main Panels
data.detail: Clear working space, locked access, labeling, thermography notes, and licensed electrician changes.

data.title: Common Lighting
data.detail: Corridors, stairs, exterior, parking, laundry, trash, emergency lighting, and bulb/fixture standards.

data.title: Unit Devices
data.detail: GFCI/AFCI issues, loose outlets, fan/light controls, range circuits, and resident repair boundaries.

data.text: Electrical work needs bright boundaries: staff can observe and document, but licensed work and local code decide who repairs.

data.title: Roof Membrane
data.detail: Punctures, blisters, seams, ponding, patches, walkway pads, contractor reports, and warranty limits.

data.title: Drains and Gutters
data.detail: Roof drains, scuppers, downspouts, leaf loads, ice risk, and overflow evidence.

data.title: Windows and Facade
data.detail: Sealant, flashing, cracks, failed balances, screens, air leaks, and recurring unit water stains.

items.text: Open work orders before dry-out hides evidence

data.text: The envelope is where small defects travel. A roof drain issue can become ceiling damage, mold risk, insurance work, and capital planning.

data.title: Parking Lot
data.detail: Potholes, striping, ADA spaces, drainage, snow storage, lighting, tow signs, and trip hazards.

data.title: Landscape
data.detail: Trees near roof or wires, irrigation leaks, erosion, pest harborage, and defensible space where applicable.

data.title: Trash and Pest Zone
data.detail: Dumpster pads, doors, bulk pickup, odors, resident misuse, vendor pickup failures, and pest logs.

data.text: Exterior maintenance affects safety, resident satisfaction, pest control, storm performance, and insurance exposure.

data.title: Pattern Watch
data.detail: Repeated calls in one line, stack, floor, appliance model, or season should become system work.

data.text: Unit work is where residents experience the maintenance system. The same work order may also reveal a building-system failure or capital need.

items.text: Smoke and CO alarms present and working
Leaks under sinks and around fixtures
Electrical covers, GFCI, and visible hazards

data.title: Wet Areas
data.detail: Bathrooms, kitchens, water heater closets, washer boxes, and ceiling stains are high-value inspection targets.

data.title: Resident Access
data.detail: Notices, appointments, pets, privacy, language needs, no-access attempts, and follow-up are part of the record.

data.text: A unit inspection is both a resident service and a building-system diagnostic. Track trends, not only pass/fail findings.

items.text: Final clean, punch, and manager sign-off

data.title: Scope Control
data.detail: Separate resident damage, normal wear, capital defects, vendor work, and rent-ready cosmetics.

data.title: Days Vacant
data.detail: Track average days from move-out to ready. Delays reveal staffing, vendor, parts, or decision bottlenecks.

data.text: Turnover should produce records useful for deposit decisions, future repairs, and maintenance planning.

data.title: Inventory
data.detail: Model, serial, age, warranty, location, repeated repair history, and spare-part compatibility.

data.title: Repair or Replace
data.detail: Use age, failure type, parts delay, resident impact, and repeated calls to decide.

data.title: Laundry Room
data.detail: Vendor equipment, lint, drains, flooring, ventilation, lighting, payment system, and resident complaints.

data.text: Appliance work looks small until patterns emerge. Records help distinguish one-off repairs from a portfolio replacement issue.

data.title: Intake
data.detail: Who, unit, issue, urgency, access permission, pets, photos, symptoms, and preferred communication channel.

data.title: Triage
data.detail: Emergency, habitability, scheduled repair, vendor needed, duplicate, resident responsibility, or capital signal.

data.title: Closeout
data.detail: What changed, who did it, photos, materials, resident notice, follow-up date, and unresolved next step.

data.text: A request is not only a task. It is a signal about resident trust, system health, and how well the team communicates.
Health and habitability views turn scattered complaints into visible patterns: moisture paths, air movement, pests, materials, and resident impact.

data.title: Source Control
data.detail: Find and stop water first: roof, plumbing, condensation, exterior grading, HVAC condensate, or resident fixture use.

data.title: Dry-Out Clock
data.detail: Fast drying, material decisions, humidity control, photos, and follow-up prevent repeat damage.

data.title: Resident Communication
data.detail: Explain access, drying equipment, containment, cleaning scope, and what will happen next.

data.text: Reference lens: EPA states that mold control is moisture control. Cleanup without source control is incomplete.

data.title: Trash Control
data.detail: Dumpster capacity, pickup misses, bulk items, chute/room cleaning, odors, resident notices, and vendor logs.

data.title: Exclusion
data.detail: Seal penetrations, sweeps, screens, pipe chases, trash doors, and exterior gaps before repeated treatment.

data.title: Treatment Log
data.detail: Unit reports, pest type, prep compliance, vendor treatment, follow-up date, and trend map.

data.text: Pest control is shared system work. The map should connect building conditions, housekeeping, vendors, and resident communication.

data.title: Ventilation
data.detail: Bath and kitchen exhaust, corridor airflow, make-up air, odors, pressure issues, and humidity complaints.

data.title: Combustion Safety
data.detail: CO alarms, gas appliances, water heaters, boilers, flues, and vendor documentation where applicable.

data.title: Radon and Smoke
data.detail: Regional radon policy, smoking complaints, infiltration paths, notices, testing records, and mitigation decisions.

data.text: Indoor air issues are often cross-system: ventilation, moisture, combustion, resident behavior, and envelope leakage can all matter.

data.title: Lead-Based Paint
data.detail: For pre-1978 buildings, keep certifications, hazard-control plans, notices, and disturbance boundaries visible.

data.title: Asbestos-Containing Materials
data.detail: Flooring, mastic, insulation, textured materials, pipe wrap, survey records, and contractor controls.

data.title: Disturbance Rules
data.detail: Staff should know when to stop, isolate, document, and call qualified professionals before cutting or sanding.

data.text: This is not legal advice. Older building material rules are local, state, and federal; the maintenance map should make the decision path clear.
Reference lens: HUD multifamily disaster planning organizes response around resident protection, building protection, and business continuity.

data.title: Incident Lead
data.detail: Decides priorities, assigns roles, tracks timeline, confirms resident safety, and escalates to ownership.

data.title: Resident Communications
data.detail: Notices, text/email, door posting, language needs, mobility needs, and update cadence.

data.title: Building Protection
data.detail: Shutoffs, temporary safeguards, vendor access, photos, security, and recovery work orders.

data.text: Use simple roles during stress. The document should answer: who leads, who communicates, who protects the building, and what is next.

items.text: Locate source and shut off water if authorized
Protect electrical and call emergency services if unsafe
Photograph damage and start affected-unit list

data.title: Affected Units
data.detail: Track stack, floor, residents, access, temporary relocation needs, contents, and follow-up repairs.

data.title: Drying and Recovery
data.detail: Restoration scope, moisture readings, demolition decisions, insurance, and final clearance notes.

data.text: The leak response view links emergency action to mold prevention, resident communication, insurance proof, and capital root-cause tracking.

items.text: Confirm utility outage or building fault
Check elevator occupancy and fire panel status

data.title: Critical Loads
data.detail: Fire alarm, emergency lighting, elevator, entry access, sump pumps, boilers, communications, and office systems.

data.title: Resident Impact
data.detail: Older adults, medical devices, mobility needs, temperature risk, and communication access determine escalation.

data.text: A power outage is both a building event and a resident-safety event. The plan must separate what staff can control from utility restoration.

items.text: Call 911 and follow fire department command
Account for affected residents when possible
Do not silence/reset systems without authorization

data.title: Fire Department Interface
data.detail: Knox/key box, fire panel, riser room, roof access, elevator recall, and building representative.

data.title: Resident Displacement
data.detail: Temporary shelter, accessible needs, medications, pets, contact list, notices, and return conditions.

data.text: The fire event view is not a substitute for emergency services. It keeps property-side responsibilities ready before and after command releases the building.

data.title: Storm Watch
data.detail: Wind, rain, flood, freeze, heat, wildfire smoke, and snow each stress different building systems.

data.title: After-Storm Walk
data.detail: Roof, facade, drains, trees, parking, leaks, power, elevator, resident reports, and photos.

data.text: Weather planning should be local. Keep regional hazards, resident vulnerabilities, and building weak points in the same nested view.

data.title: Immediate Repairs
data.detail: Life-safety concerns, deferred maintenance, and active damage should not wait for annual budgeting.

data.text: Capital planning turns repeated work orders, inspections, useful-life estimates, and photos into a defensible replacement path.

data.title: Roof
data.detail: Age, type, warranty, patches, leak history, contractor, drain condition, and replacement window.

data.title: Elevator
data.detail: Controller, cab, door equipment, service history, violations, modernization needs, and downtime.

data.title: Mechanical
data.detail: Boilers, water heaters, pumps, air handlers, exhaust fans, age, condition, and service notes.

data.text: An asset register lets maintenance, ownership, lenders, and vendors talk about the same physical components.

data.title: Useful Life
data.detail: Remaining useful life should be updated when inspections, failures, or major repairs change the risk picture.

data.title: Replacement Reserve
data.detail: Set aside funds for components that wear out: roof, HVAC, paving, elevators, appliances, and common areas.

data.title: Required Repairs
data.detail: Deferred maintenance and life-safety concerns need clear scope, owner, cost, date, and proof of completion.

items.text: Prioritize life-safety and water damage risk

data.text: Reference lens: property condition assessments connect physical condition, immediate repairs, capital items, and reserves.

data.title: Year 1
data.detail: Correct life-safety gaps, restore roof drains, tag shutoffs, and close deferred maintenance with photos.

data.title: Years 2-3
data.detail: Plan water heater replacements, corridor lighting upgrades, parking repairs, and targeted unit ventilation work.

data.title: Years 4-5
data.detail: Prepare roof replacement, elevator modernization study, facade repairs, and reserve adjustment.

data.text: The five-year plan should be updated by evidence. Canaster hierarchy helps connect a small recurring issue to the larger capital story.
Records are operational tools, not paperwork. They let a future manager understand what happened, what changed, and what still needs attention.

data.title: Plumber
data.detail: Emergency line, account number, after-hours terms, shutoff authority, and standard response notes.

data.title: Fire Protection Vendor
data.detail: Alarm, sprinkler, extinguisher, inspection schedule, monitoring account, and impairment contact.

data.title: Elevator Vendor
data.detail: Service line, callback process, entrapment escalation, contract scope, and inspector contacts.

data.text: Vendor records should be useful at 2 a.m. during an emergency, not only during office hours.

data.title: Report Intake
data.detail: Scan, name, tag, assign owner, extract deficiencies, due dates, and required filings.

data.title: Correction Tracking
data.detail: Each deficiency needs a work order, responsible person, evidence, and closeout date.

data.title: Photo Proof
data.detail: Before, during, after, label, unit/common area, date, and link to report item.

data.text: A report is only useful when deficiencies become tracked work and corrections become retrievable proof.

data.title: Keys and Access
data.detail: Master keys, fobs, lockbox, vendor keys, sign-out log, lost key procedure, and restricted areas.

data.title: Tools
data.detail: Serial numbers, assigned users, storage location, calibration needs, and theft/loss reporting.

data.title: Supplies
data.detail: Filters, lamps, batteries, door hardware, plumbing parts, PPE, ice melt, and emergency stock.

data.text: HUD management review expectations include inventory systems for tools, equipment, supplies, and keys. This view makes that tangible.

data.title: HUD NSPIRE
data.detail: Health, safety, functional defects, resident focus, and year-round maintenance practices.

data.title: HUD Management Review
data.detail: Preventive schedules, unit inspections, work orders, emergency orders, inventory, and backlog.

data.title: Property Maintenance Code
data.detail: Exterior/interior conditions, sanitation, plumbing, mechanical, electrical, elevators, egress, and fire safety.

data.title: EPA Mold and Legionella
data.detail: Moisture control, mold prevention, water temperature, flushing, and water management programs.

data.title: ASHRAE Multifamily
data.detail: HVAC operation, maintenance, ventilation, and airflow guidance for multifamily buildings.

data.title: Disaster Planning
data.detail: Resident protection, building protection, business continuity, staff roles, and communication.

data.text: This starter is a practical operations document, not legal advice. A real property must confirm local code, fire marshal rules, elevator jurisdiction, lease obligations, and licensed-contractor requirements.
